\chapter{The Other Way to Count}
\label{ch:ja-native-count-one-to-five}
\hlchaptermodality{16}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can count things from one to five in the native Japanese series, write the two signs it cost, and say the one place where the same word stands in both of Japanese's counts.}

Run hitotsu to itsutsu, say the borrowed five beside them, and name the one number where a single word appears in both counts.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[hi]{\ja{ひ} — one stroke, and a second count begins}

\label{lesson:JA-W16-hi}



\begin{quote}
Three recalls, then one sign.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} write \textbf{\ja{ろ}} — \textbf{R2}, five lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{ten}, then build \emph{thirteen} and \emph{thirty} from it — \textbf{R2}, five lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{more, again} — \textbf{R4}, eighty lessons back
\end{itemize}

Last chapter bought two signs for a count of ten. This chapter buys five, for a count of ten that Japanese runs \textbf{beside} the one you already have.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script — the shape}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ja{ひ}} — \emph{hi}
\end{quote}

One stroke, and the KanjiVG stroke data for this sign holds exactly one path: start high on the left, run a short way to the right, then sweep down and far to the left in a long shallow curve and finish by turning up. The pen does not lift once.

Compare \textbf{\ja{ろ}}, which you wrote five lessons ago: also one stroke, but \textbf{\ja{ろ}} closes its loop and \textbf{\ja{ひ}} never closes at all.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{enumerate}
\raggedright
  \item Trace \textbf{\ja{ひ}} once and copy it once, without lifting.
  \item Hide it; write it after ten seconds.
  \item Write \textbf{\ja{ろ}} and \textbf{\ja{ひ}} side by side: one closes, one does not.
\end{enumerate}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How many strokes? (\textbf{One.})

Source: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U3040.pdf}{Unicode Hiragana chart}; stroke count and order per \href{https://kanjivg.tagaini.net/kanjivg/kanji/03072.html}{KanjiVG}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[hitotsu]{\ja{ひとつ} — one thing}

\label{lesson:JA-C16-hitotsu}



\begin{quote}
Three recalls, then the first word of a second count.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} write \textbf{\ja{ひ}} — \textbf{R1}, one lesson back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{six} — \textbf{R2}, five lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} write \textbf{\ja{も}} — \textbf{R4}, eighty lessons back
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll Want to Know — hear and say}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ja{ひとつ}} — \emph{hi-to-tsu} — \textbf{one thing}
\end{quote}

Three beats, three signs: \textbf{\ja{ひ}} from last lesson, \textbf{\ja{と}} and \textbf{\ja{つ}} long since yours.

You already have a word for \emph{one}. It is \textbf{\ja{いち}}, and it is borrowed. \textbf{\ja{ひとつ}} is the word Japanese had before it borrowed anything, and the two are not interchangeable:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{word} & \textbf{what it is for} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\ja{いち}} & the number itself — \emph{one}, counting aloud, a house number \\
\textbf{\ja{ひとつ}} & \textbf{one thing} — a thing you are pointing at \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Wiktionary's usage note for \textbf{\ja{ひとつ}} is one sentence and it is the sentence this chapter turns on: it is used \emph{when the items counted have no specific counter category}. Hold that. It will be the whole of the next chapter.

\subsection*{Your turn — read, copy, recall}
Write \textbf{\ja{ひとつ}}. Say \emph{ichi}, then \emph{hitotsu}, and hear that they share nothing — not a beat, not a sound.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which of the two words is the borrowed one? (\textbf{\ja{いち}}.)

Sources: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%E4\%B8\%80\%E3\%81\%A4}{Wiktionary: hitotsu}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[fu]{\ja{ふ} — four strokes, and a counter you already own}

\label{lesson:JA-W16-fu}



\begin{quote}
Three recalls, then one sign.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{one thing} — \textbf{R1}, one lesson back
  \item \emph{Recall:} write the small \textbf{\ja{ゅ}} — \textbf{R2}, five lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{one time} — \textbf{R4}, eighty lessons back
\end{itemize}

\textbf{\ja{いちど}} is worth stopping on. Its own lesson said \emph{do counts an occurrence} — which is to say \textbf{\ja{いちど} is a number with a counter behind it}, and you have been saying it since chapter nine without anyone calling it that. Two chapters from now that sentence is the whole point.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script — the shape}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ja{ふ}} — \emph{fu}
\end{quote}

Four separate strokes, in this order, as KanjiVG records them: a short tick at the top; then the body, starting below it and curving down and to the left; then a small mark low on the left; then a small mark low on the right.

Everything this book has taught you so far has been one, two or three strokes. This is the first sign with four, and the last two are easy to run together by accident. They are separate.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{enumerate}
\raggedright
  \item Trace \textbf{\ja{ふ}} once, counting the four lifts aloud.
  \item Copy it once; hide it; write it again.
  \item Check only one thing: are the bottom two marks separate?
\end{enumerate}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How many strokes? (\textbf{Four.})

Source: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U3040.pdf}{Unicode Hiragana chart}; stroke count and order per \href{https://kanjivg.tagaini.net/kanjivg/kanji/03075.html}{KanjiVG}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[futatsu]{\ja{ふたつ} — two things}

\label{lesson:JA-C16-futatsu}



\begin{quote}
Four recalls, then the second thing.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} write \textbf{\ja{ふ}}, all four strokes — \textbf{R1}, one lesson back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{ten}, then \emph{twenty} — \textbf{R2}, five lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{please} — \textbf{R4}, eighty lessons back
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll Want to Know — hear and say}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ja{ふたつ}} — \emph{fu-ta-tsu} — \textbf{two things}
\end{quote}

Three signs, and the only new one arrived last lesson.

Now hear the two words together: \textbf{\ja{ひとつ}}, \textbf{\ja{ふたつ}}. Both end in \textbf{\ja{つ}}, and the part in front changes — \emph{hito-}, \emph{futa-}. That \textbf{\ja{つ}} is not decoration. It is the piece doing the counting, and every word in this chapter but the last one carries it.

\textbf{\ja{に}} is \emph{two}. \textbf{\ja{ふたつ}} is \emph{two things}. Same relation as \textbf{\ja{いち}} and \textbf{\ja{ひとつ}}, and again the two words share nothing at all.

\subsection*{Your turn — read, copy, recall}
Write \textbf{\ja{ふたつ}}. Say the pair: \emph{hitotsu, futatsu}. Then say \emph{ichi, ni} straight after, and hear two different counts running side by side.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does the \textbf{\ja{つ}} do? (\textbf{It counts.})

Sources: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%E4\%BA\%8C\%E3\%81\%A4}{Wiktionary: futatsu}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[mittsu]{\ja{みっつ} — three things, for nothing}

\label{lesson:JA-C16-mittsu}



\begin{quote}
Three recalls, then a word that costs nothing.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{two things} — \textbf{R1}, one lesson back
  \item \emph{Recall:} run the family reception — \textbf{R3}, twenty lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{one more time, please} — \textbf{R4}, eighty lessons back
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll Want to Know — hear and say}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ja{みっつ}} — \emph{mi-t-tsu} — \textbf{three things}
\end{quote}

Every sign is already yours: \textbf{\ja{み}}, the small \textbf{\ja{っ}}, and \textbf{\ja{つ}}.

The small \textbf{\ja{っ}} is the sign you met in \textbf{\ja{ゆっくり}}: it holds the mouth shut for one beat. \textbf{\ja{みっつ}} is three beats, and the middle one is silence.

\textbf{\ja{さん}} is \emph{three}. \textbf{\ja{みっつ}} is \emph{three things}.

\subsection*{Your turn — read, copy, recall}
Write \textbf{\ja{みっつ}}. Say the run so far, slowly: \emph{hitotsu, futatsu, mittsu}. Stop on the silent beat in the third one.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How many signs did this word cost? (\textbf{None} — all three were yours.)

Sources: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%E4\%B8\%89\%E3\%81\%A4}{Wiktionary: mittsu}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[yottsu]{\ja{よっつ} — four things, and the seam opens}

\label{lesson:JA-C16-yottsu}



\begin{quote}
Three recalls, then the number that has been in both counts all along.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{three things} — \textbf{R1}, one lesson back
  \item \emph{Recall:} run the nine family words — \textbf{R3}, twenty lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} write \textbf{\ja{せ}} — \textbf{R4}, eighty lessons back
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll Want to Know — hear and say}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ja{よっつ}} — \emph{yo-t-tsu} — \textbf{four things}
\end{quote}

No new sign. \textbf{\ja{よ}}, the small \textbf{\ja{っ}}, \textbf{\ja{つ}}.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens — the seam, from the other side}]
Chapter fourteen taught \textbf{\ja{よん}} and said something that was left hanging: \emph{that split is coming back; it is the same seam the counters run along.} Here it is.

\textbf{\ja{よん}} is a native word standing inside the borrowed count. \textbf{\ja{よっつ}} is that same native word in the count it belongs to. They begin with the same beat, and that is not an accident — it is one word appearing twice:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{number} & \textbf{borrowed} & \textbf{native} \\
\midrule
one & \ja{いち} & \ja{ひと}- \\
two & \ja{に} & \ja{ふた}- \\
three & \ja{さん} & \ja{み}- \\
\textbf{four} & \emph{shi} & \textbf{\ja{よ}-} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Every other line of the borrowed column is genuinely borrowed. At four, the native word came across into the borrowed count and stayed — which is why the number you actually say for four is \textbf{\ja{よん}} and not \emph{shi}. That is what chapter fourteen was pointing at, and you can now see both halves of it at once.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn — read, copy, recall}
Write \textbf{\ja{よっつ}}. Say \emph{yon}, then \emph{yottsu}, and hear the shared beat. Then say \emph{shi} and hear that it has none.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which two words share a beat? (\textbf{\ja{よん}} and \textbf{\ja{よっつ}}.)

Sources: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%E5\%9B\%9B\%E3\%81\%A4}{Wiktionary: yottsu}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[itsutsu]{\ja{いつつ} — five things}

\label{lesson:JA-C16-itsutsu}



\begin{quote}
Three recalls, then five.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{four things} — \textbf{R1}, one lesson back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{one} — \textbf{R3}, twenty lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} write \textbf{\ja{お}} — \textbf{R4}, eighty lessons back
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll Want to Know — hear and say}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ja{いつつ}} — \emph{i-tsu-tsu} — \textbf{five things}
\end{quote}

Three signs, and two of them are the same one. \textbf{\ja{い}}, \textbf{\ja{つ}}, \textbf{\ja{つ}}.

A warning worth one sentence: \textbf{\ja{いつつ}} opens on the same beat as \textbf{\ja{いち}}, and the two have nothing to do with each other. \textbf{\ja{ご}} is \emph{five}; \textbf{\ja{いつつ}} is \emph{five things}; \textbf{\ja{いち}} is \emph{one}. The ear will try to pair the wrong two.

\subsection*{Your turn — read, copy, recall}
Write \textbf{\ja{いつつ}}. Say \emph{ichi} and \emph{itsutsu} back to back, then \emph{go} and \emph{itsutsu}, and fix which pair actually means the same number.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which number does \textbf{\ja{いつつ}} NOT mean? (\textbf{One} — however it starts.)

Sources: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%E4\%BA\%94\%E3\%81\%A4}{Wiktionary: itsutsu}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{Five things, and five numbers}

\label{lesson:JA-R16-first-five-things}



\begin{quote}
Three recalls, then the run.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{five things} — \textbf{R1}, one lesson back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{one thing} — \textbf{R2}, six lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{I understood} — \textbf{R4}, eighty lessons back
\end{itemize}

Nothing new arrives here.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn — the run}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{ichi, hitotsu; ni, futatsu; san, mittsu; yon, yottsu; go, itsutsu}
  \item \emph{Write it:} \textbf{\ja{ひ}} and \textbf{\ja{ふ}} — the two signs this chapter bought
\end{itemize}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built so far}]
Five words for \textbf{two signs}. \textbf{\ja{ひ}} and \textbf{\ja{ふ}} were bought in the lessons immediately before the words that needed them; \textbf{\ja{みっつ}}, \textbf{\ja{よっつ}} and \textbf{\ja{いつつ}} cost nothing, because every sign in them was already yours.

Two counts of five now run side by side, and they share exactly one thing: at \textbf{four}, \textbf{\ja{よん}} and \textbf{\ja{よっつ}} begin with the same beat. Everywhere else the two words have nothing in common — \emph{ichi} and \emph{hitotsu}, \emph{ni} and \emph{futatsu}, and so on down.

Five more to go, and three more signs.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How many signs did these five words cost? (\textbf{Two.}) Where do the two counts touch? (\textbf{At four.})
\end{tcolorbox}
